title: OOP internals
scopeHtml: Scope: object memory layout, vtables and dispatch, constructor order, equals/hashCode contract, immutability and defensive copies. Questions are still to be written.

notes.title: What an object is in memory
notes.html:
An object is a block of bytes on the heap; a variable holds a reference (an address-like handle) to it. Copying a reference copies the handle, not the object. This one fact explains aliasing bugs, == vs equals, and defensive copies.

On HotSpot (64-bit) an object has a header then fields:

  • Mark word: 8 bytes (hash code, GC age, lock state).
  • Class pointer: 4 bytes with compressed oops (default for heaps under about 32 GB), else 8.
  • Fields, aligned; total size rounded up to a multiple of 8.
class Point { int x; int y; }

offset  size  content
0       8     mark word
8       4     class pointer (compressed)
12      4     x
16      4     y
20      4     padding -> total 24 bytes

Worked example. One million Point objects = 24 MB of objects plus the array of references (4 MB with compressed oops) = 28 MB. A primitive int[] pair (int[] xs, ys) holds the same data in 8 MB. This is why games and Android code avoid millions of tiny objects (GC pressure, cache misses).

Industry examples. Android's SparseArray and IntArray avoid boxing; Kotlin value class and Java's Project Valhalla (value types, in progress; confirm status for your JDK) aim to remove headers. Tools: JOL (Java Object Layout) prints real layouts.

Everyday analogy. A variable is a sticky note with a locker number. Copying the note gives two notes for one locker.

Common interview traps.

  • "Java passes objects by reference." It passes references by value; reassigning the parameter does not change the caller's variable.
  • Forgetting boxing: an Integer is about 16 bytes versus a 4-byte int.
  • == compares references, not contents.

notes.title: Virtual dispatch and vtables
notes.html:
When you call a.speak() and a might be a Dog or Cat, the JVM picks the method at runtime. That is dynamic dispatch (polymorphism).

Mechanism: each class has a vtable, an array of method pointers. A subclass copies its parent's table and replaces overridden slots. a.speak() becomes "load class pointer, index slot k, jump". Cost: one extra indirection. HotSpot's JIT usually removes it: if only one class is loaded for a call site it inlines (monomorphic); with two it checks type (bimorphic); beyond that it uses the vtable (megamorphic, slower, no inlining).

Animal vtable:  [0]=Animal.speak  [1]=Animal.eat
Dog vtable:     [0]=Dog.speak     [1]=Animal.eat     (overrides slot 0)
Animal a = new Dog();
a.speak();       // dispatched on the runtime class (Dog)
open class Animal { open fun speak() = "..." }
class Dog : Animal() { override fun speak() = "Woof" }

What is NOT virtual. static, private, final methods and constructors are bound at compile time. Fields are never polymorphic: they use the declared type ("field hiding"). Kotlin classes and members are final by default; Java's are open by default.

Worked example. static call: 0 dispatch cost. Monomorphic virtual call: about 0 after inlining. A megamorphic interface call over 5 implementations in a hot loop may cost 3 to 5 ns extra per call; for 100M calls that is 0.3 to 0.5 s.

Industry examples. Android ART does devirtualization too. Kotlin's final default and sealed classes help the compiler. interface calls use itables (slightly slower than class vtables in older JVMs).

Everyday analogy. A phone book per department: you look up "speak" in the Dog's own book.

Common interview traps.

  • Overloading is resolved at compile time on the declared types; overriding at runtime.
  • Calling an overridable method from a constructor (next section).
  • Thinking private methods can be overridden; they cannot.

notes.title: Constructor order and initialization
notes.html:
Java builds an object parent first, then child. For new Child():

  1. Memory is allocated and zeroed (all fields default 0/null/false).
  2. Child() starts and calls super(...) first (explicitly or implicitly).
  3. The parent runs its field initializers and instance blocks, then its constructor body.
  4. Then the child's field initializers and instance blocks, then the child constructor body.

Static initializers run once per class at class initialization, parent first, before any instance.

class Parent {
    Parent() { System.out.println("Parent ctor"); init(); }
    void init() { System.out.println("Parent init"); }
}
class Child extends Parent {
    private String name = "child";
    Child() { System.out.println("Child ctor, name=" + name); }
    @Override void init() { System.out.println("Child init, name=" + name); }
}
// new Child() prints:
// Parent ctor
// Child init, name=null     <- field not yet assigned!
// Child ctor, name=child
open class Parent { init { println("Parent init"); hook() }; open fun hook() {} }
class Child : Parent() {
    private val name = "child"
    override fun hook() { println("name=$name") }   // prints name=null
}

Worked example. The bug: an overridden method called from the parent constructor sees null or 0 in child fields; a NullPointerException at startup that "works in tests with a mock". Cost to debug: hours.

Rule. Never call overridable methods from a constructor. Make it final/private, or use a factory or a separate init() called after construction.

Industry examples. Android View constructors calling overridable onFinishInflate-like hooks; frameworks like Spring use @PostConstruct precisely to run after full construction.

Everyday analogy. You must pour the foundation before the walls: the parent builds its part before the child exists.

Common interview traps.

  • Predicting output order; practise this exact snippet.
  • this(...) and super(...) must be the first statement (relaxed in newer Java previews; confirm version).
  • Kotlin lateinit / property initialization order in the primary constructor.

notes.title: equals and hashCode contract
notes.html:
If you override equals, you must override hashCode. HashMap and HashSet find an object by hashCode first (picks the bucket), then equals (confirms). Break the pair and lookups silently fail.

The equals contract: reflexive (x.equals(x)), symmetric, transitive, consistent over time, and x.equals(null) is false. The hashCode contract: equal objects must have equal hash codes; unequal objects may share a hash (collisions) but should spread out.

final class Money {
    private final long cents; private final String currency;
    Money(long c, String cur) { cents = c; currency = cur; }
    @Override public boolean equals(Object o) {
        if (this == o) return true;
        if (!(o instanceof Money m)) return false;
        return cents == m.cents && currency.equals(m.currency);
    }
    @Override public int hashCode() { return java.util.Objects.hash(cents, currency); }
}
data class Money(val cents: Long, val currency: String)   // equals/hashCode/toString generated

Worked example. A User with equals on id but no hashCode: set.add(u1); set.contains(new User(sameId)) returns false 15 of 16 times (default identity hash lands in another bucket of a 16-bucket table). Intermittent, hence nasty.

Pitfalls. Mutable fields in hashCode: mutate a key after inserting it and the entry becomes unreachable (a leak). Inheritance and equals with instanceof breaks symmetry (Point vs ColorPoint); prefer final classes or composition. Avoid floating == in equals (use Double.compare). JPA entities: equality on a generated id that is null before save is a known trap.

Industry examples. Effective Java (Bloch) items 10 and 11; Lombok @EqualsAndHashCode; Kotlin data classes; Guava Objects. Java 8 HashMap converts long buckets (8+ entries) to trees, so bad hashes cost O(log n) instead of O(n) but still hurt.

Everyday analogy. The hash is the building and floor; equals is checking the apartment's name plate. Wrong building, you never find them.

Common interview traps.

  • Overriding one but not the other.
  • Using mutable fields as hash keys.
  • equals(Foo f) instead of equals(Object o): that is an overload, not an override. @Override catches it.

notes.title: Immutability
notes.html:
An immutable object never changes after construction. Safe to share between threads without locks, safe as a map key, and easy to reason about.

Recipe: final class (or private constructor), all fields private final, no setters, no leaking mutable internals (copy in, copy out), do not let this escape from the constructor.

public final class Event {
    private final String name; private final Instant at; private final List<String> tags;
    public Event(String name, Instant at, List<String> tags) {
        this.name = name; this.at = at;
        this.tags = List.copyOf(tags);          // defensive copy, also immutable
    }
    public List<String> tags() { return tags; }  // safe: already unmodifiable
    public Event withName(String n) { return new Event(n, at, tags); }   // "wither"
}
data class Event(val name: String, val at: Instant, val tags: List<String>)
val e2 = e1.copy(name = "new")    // copy instead of mutate

Worked example. String is immutable, so its hash is cached; a 1 M entry HashMap<String,...> computes each hash once. Sharing one Config across 200 threads needs zero locks. Cost: each "change" allocates a new object (e.g. building a string in a loop of 100,000 with + is O(n squared); use StringBuilder).

Industry examples. String, Integer, java.time, BigDecimal, Kotlin val and read-only collections, Redux-style UI state, Compose state, immutable messages in Kafka.

Decision gravity. Starting immutable is cheap; making a mutable class immutable later breaks every setter caller (one-way door). Mutable is justified for hot paths and builders.

Everyday analogy. A printed receipt: to change it, you issue a new receipt.

Common interview traps.

  • final on a field does not make the object immutable; the list inside can still change.
  • Kotlin List is a read-only view, not necessarily immutable; the backing MutableList may still change.
  • Forgetting to make the class final so a subclass adds mutability.

notes.title: Defensive copies
notes.html:
A defensive copy is a private duplicate you make so outside code cannot change your internals. Needed at two points: when you receive a mutable argument and when you return a mutable field.

class Booking {
    private final Date start;                       // Date is mutable (legacy)
    Booking(Date start) { this.start = new Date(start.getTime()); }   // copy in
    Date start() { return new Date(start.getTime()); }               // copy out
}
// Without copies: Date d = new Date(); Booking b = new Booking(d); d.setTime(0);  // corrupts b!
class Roster(players: List<String>) {
    private val players = players.toList()          // copy in
    fun all(): List<String> = players.toList()      // copy out (or expose read-only view)
}

Worked example. A Cart returns its internal ArrayList of 100 items. A UI bug calls .clear() on it; the cart silently empties. Copying costs 100 pointer copies (about 0.3 microseconds), negligible against the bug.

Cheaper options. Collections.unmodifiableList(list) is a view (no copy, but changes to the backing list show through); List.copyOf makes a real immutable copy (no copy if already immutable); use immutable types (java.time) and you need no copies.

Shallow vs deep. Copying a list copies references; if elements are mutable, the elements are still shared. Copy elements too, or make them immutable.

Industry examples. JDK's Arrays.asList is a fixed-size view over the array (writes pass through); Android Bundle/Intent extras and Parcelable copy across processes.

Everyday analogy. You give a friend a photocopy of your key list, not the original keys.

Common interview traps.

  • Copying in the getter but not in the constructor (or vice versa).
  • Shallow copy of nested mutable objects.
  • Performance panic: copies are usually cheap; measure first.
  • clone(): widely discouraged; prefer copy constructors or factories.

notes.title: Summary
notes.html:
• An object = header (mark word 8 B, class pointer 4 B) + fields, padded to 8 B; variables hold references, passed by value.
  • Virtual calls use vtables; static/private/final are bound at compile time; JIT inlines monomorphic sites.
  • Construction order: zeroed memory, parent init and ctor, child init and ctor; never call overridable methods in a constructor.
  • Override equals and hashCode together; use immutable fields in the hash; mind the equals(Object) signature.
  • Immutability: final class, final private fields, no setters, copy mutable inputs/outputs; Kotlin val and read-only List are not deep immutability.
  • Defensive copies at the boundary (copy in, copy out); prefer immutable types to avoid them.
